In this Across Acoustics episode, recorded on April 22, 2024, host Kat Setzer talks with Efren Fernandez-Grande, an associate professor at the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) and JASA associate editor, and DTU PhD student Xenofon Karakonstantis. Sound field reconstruction estimates the whole field in a space, including pressure, particle velocity and intensity, from arrays or scattered measurement points. It serves sound radiation, noise source identification, room acoustics, audio capture and material characterization. The catch is bandwidth: audible wavelengths in air run from 17 m to 17 mm, so low frequencies need large apertures and high frequencies sensors only millimeters apart. More sensors add cost and complexity and scatter the field, and small changes, like moving a chair, alter it anyway. Sparse methods such as compressed sensing struggle in rooms, where many waves overlap.

Their answer is generative adversarial networks (GANs), in which a generator produces samples and a discriminator judges whether they look real. They compared three bandwidth-extension models: a conventional GAN trained unsupervised on room impulse response datasets, and a conditional GAN and HiFi-GAN adapted from speech bandwidth extension and trained on simulated data. HiFi-GAN performed best, preserving high-frequency magnitude thanks to multiple discriminators for different bands.

The output is statistically plausible, not the room’s true response, which is why Fernandez-Grande calls it “faking”: like a generative model restoring the cropped branches of a tree photo, the result looks right but is not the original. The team is now developing physics-informed neural networks that constrain results to the wave equation.

Adapted into Chinese by Fanyu Meng from the Across Acoustics episode “Deep Faking Room Impulse Responses,” in which Kat Setzer interviews Efren Fernandez-Grande and Xenofon Karakonstantis about their JASA paper “Generative models for sound field reconstruction” (ASA Publications, 2024). Listen to the original.
